newsitem.title: ITALY: Italy's railway boss apologises for weekend chaos.
newsitem.headline: Italy's railway boss apologises for weekend chaos.

text.p: The head of Italy's state railways apologised on Monday to tens of thousands of passengers affected by a weekend of chaos on the trains and said much must be done to get the nation's rail network up to speed.
"I apologize to the passengers. Italy's railways are in a backward situation. We have to do much to raise the quality level," president of the state railway Giancarlo Cimoli said.

Travellers were stranded in stations for up to 12 hours or forced to board crowded buses after a train derailed in Rome on Saturday and then a crane working to remove it collapsed onto tracks that pass through Italy's main north-south rail artery.
Four passengers suffered minor injuries from the derailment, which happened as thousands of Italians took off for their summer holidays in one of the busiest weekends of the year for the railroads.
Travel was still disrupted throughout the day on Monday, as engineers struggled to clear the crucial tracks.

Union leaders and members of the centre-right parliamentary opposition bloc heaped criticism on Transport Minister Claudio Burlando and railway officials, with the far-right party National Alliance demanding the minister's resignation.
Consumer groups demanded the railways reimburse each affected traveller with one million lire ($550).
Burlando said in an interview published in La Repubblica newspaper on Monday that Italy's railway network "faces an infrastructural and technological delay that has perhaps no equal in Europe."
At a news conference later in the day he said the government planned in the next three years to invest 42 trillion lire ($23 billion) to renovate the rail system.

The money will be used in particular to introduce an automatic traffic control system on the nation's main lines and to quadruple the number of tracks connecting northern and southern Italy within the next five years.
"It is difficult to control the traffic of the year 2000 with structures that go back to 1800," Burlando said.
He stressed that despite technological delays, the safety of Italy's trains was not to be doubted.
"The number of casualties in rail accidents in Italy is fewer than in the main European countries," the minister said.
Eight people died last January when a Milan-Rome high speed train derailed near the northern city of Piacenza.
Investigators suspected excess speed caused that accident and newspapers reported that Saturday's derailment might also have been caused by speeding.
